comparedAgainst: https://www.cloudflare.com/learning/ssl/what-happens-in-a-tls-handshake/ (fetch blocked, HTTP 403; known from general knowledge to be conceptual, code-free marketing/learning-center prose)
justification: Compared against the kind of page that actually ranks for 'how https works': MDN's Transport Layer Security page (confirmed by fetching it directly) has no runnable code of any kind, covers the handshake only as four bullet points ('agree on TLS version', 'agree on cipher suite', 'optional mutual auth', 'agree on a secret key') with no ClientHello/EncryptedExtensions/CertificateVerify/Finished detail, links RFC 8446 once with zero direct quotes, and never mentions or corrects the older RSA-key-exchange story. Cloudflare's handshake explainer blocked the fetch (403) but is known to be the same genre: conceptual, no code, no RFC text. Against that bar this article's differentiator is real: three from-scratch C# programs that make AEAD confidentiality/integrity, ECDH key agreement, and ECDSA/HMAC authentication empirically observable (flip a tag byte, watch `AuthenticationTagMismatchException`; derive the same secret on both sides without transmitting it; sign, then fail verification after either the transcript or the key changes), a message-by-message handshake walkthrough with an SVG sequence diagram, and an explicit, RFC-quoted correction of the RSA-key-exchange misconception the task brief asked for. `node tools/run-code.mjs src/content/articles/networking/tls-and-https.md` passes (PASS, blocks=14, executed=7). Source accuracy is strong: I fetched RFC 8446 sections 1, 1.2, 2, 4.4.2, 4.4.3 and 4.4.4, RFC 5280 section 3.2, the Let's Encrypt FAQ, and all seven distinct Microsoft Learn pages the article quotes (AesGcm.Decrypt Remarks, AuthenticationTagMismatchException, ECDiffieHellman.DeriveKeyFromHash, ECDsa.SignHash, SslStream.RemoteCertificate, RemoteCertificateValidationCallback, X509Chain Remarks) and every quoted phrase matches the live source verbatim, including the two RFC 8446 sentences (CertificateVerify's and Finished's definitions) that the RFC repeats near-identically in both section 2's overview and the cited 4.4.x sections, and the Let's Encrypt phishing/malware answer, which I confirmed in full ('...which are able to more effectively protect users'). Sibling-overlap check: I grepped `http-explained.md` for TLS/certificate/handshake terms and found nothing, so no overlap there. I read `how-the-internet-works.md`'s Band 3 section in full: it already establishes the three RFC 8446 properties, a three-flight handshake summary (ClientHello/ServerHello/Finished) naming SNI, ALPN, the certificate and its signature, and one sentence correcting the RSA-key-exchange misconception. This article's own intro explicitly frames itself as going 'one level lower' than that, and the added detail (EncryptedExtensions as a separate message, the CertificateVerify/Finished split, AEAD internals, ECDH internals) is genuinely new rather than restated — but the specific RSA-key-exchange correction, which the task names as this article's differentiator, is also already present as one sentence in the sibling, so it is not exclusively this article's territory; a reader of both pillar articles in order sees that specific myth-busting point twice. What keeps this below a pass: two sources listed in front matter — 'AesGcm Class' (`system.security.cryptography.aesgcm`) and 'HMACSHA256.HashData Method' (`system.security.cryptography.hmacsha256.hashdata`) — are never cited inline anywhere in the body, even though both types are used in running code and discussed in prose; every other citation in the article is accurate and well-scoped, which is a real improvement over the pilot findings but does not excuse leaving two full sources unused. That is exactly the binding-lesson finding docs/EDITORIAL_BRIEF.md calls out ('A source in the list that is never cited inline... is a finding'), just doubled. One more minor issue on the myth-busting overlap rounds out the list.
